voiceover.text: So, why don't good intentions turn into exercise? Earlier, you named this gap. Now, why it happens, and the full fix. Two people decide in January to run three times a week. Both mean it. Person A tells everyone, buys good shoes, and plans to run whenever she gets the chance. Person B tells nobody, keeps her old shoes, and writes on the fridge: Tuesday and Thursday at seven, Sunday at four, from the front door, twenty minutes, whatever the weather. By March, B is still running. A stopped in week three. A had more motivation, better gear and a public promise. Why wasn't that enough?

Knowing exercise is good isn't the problem. Almost everyone knows, which is why information campaigns change so little. Even intending isn't enough. In exercise studies, close to half of the people who intend to exercise don't follow through. Three things sit in the gap. The decision gets reopened every day, and each time is a chance to lose. The costs are today, and the benefits are years away. And nothing reminds you. That's why self-regulation matters: setting your own goals, checking what you actually do, and adjusting. It runs in three phases: set, monitor, evaluate.

Set comes first, and the kind of goal matters more than its size. An outcome goal is a result, like winning the district final. It depends on opponents and luck, so you can do everything right and still miss it. A performance goal is a personal standard, like five kilometres in under twenty-five minutes. A process goal is an action you fully control, like three runs this week. That's the one that changes behaviour. Only you can fail it, and it gives you a win every week, which feeds competence. Make it specific, measurable, reachable but challenging, and time-bound.

scenes.title: decide once: when, where and how

voiceover.text: Then make it concrete. An implementation intention names when, where and how. That's B's fridge note, and it fixes all three problems. The decision is made once, on a calm day, so Tuesday at seven isn't a choice any more. The time and place become the cue. And there's nothing left to plan on the day. Stronger still, hook it onto something that already happens: I get off the bus two stops early and walk the rest. And A's advantages? Motivation forms the intention, but it doesn't get you out the door on a cold morning, and new shoes can feel like starting without being it.

scenes.title: monitor, then evaluate: the same week, two futures

voiceover.text: Phase two is self-monitoring: recording what you actually did. Memory flatters us. People remember more sessions than their records show. And just recording a behaviour tends to change it, because a gap you can see is hard to ignore. Phase three is self-evaluation: comparing what you did with the plan, and deciding what it means. This is where most attempts die. Take one missed week. One person says, I missed three sessions because I've got no discipline. That attribution, the reason you give yourself, is personal and permanent, so next week looks hopeless, and she stops. Another says, I missed them because it was exam week. That's specific and temporary, so she starts again. Same week, opposite futures. And if a cause really is permanent, change the plan, not the person.

So plan for relapse, a slide back to the old habit, because everyone has a bad stretch. Earlier, you saw a missed day is data, not a verdict. Add two things. If-then plans for the obstacles you can see coming: if it's raining, then twenty minutes indoors. And a restart that's easier than where you stopped, because starting again is harder than keeping going.

Self-regulation isn't only about turning up. It's a performance skill too. A self-regulating athlete sets her own goal for each session, watches her own execution, judges it honestly, and adjusts. That's the error detection of the autonomous stage, and the reason good coaches fade their feedback. An athlete who can't self-regulate improves only while the coach is watching. One who can improves in every hour she trains.
Two things to remember. Decide once: when, where and how. And blame the plan, not the person.

Two exam questions. First. A netballer writes three goals. One: win the grand final. Two: raise my shooting percentage from seventy to eighty by August. Three: take fifty extra shots after every Tuesday and Thursday training. Classify each goal, and explain which is most useful for changing her behaviour week to week. Pause here to answer.

One is an outcome goal, because it depends on opponents. Two is a performance goal, a personal standard. Three is a process goal, fully in her control, and it's the most useful week to week, because only she can fail it, and every completed session counts as a win. The classic mistake is choosing the grand final because it's the most motivating.

scenes.title: attempt two (every day for a year)

voiceover.text: Second. A student writes: I'm going to run every single day for a year without missing one. If I miss a day, I'll start the count again. Explain why this plan is likely to fail, even though it's specific and in her control, and rewrite it. Pause here to answer.

It has no plan for a lapse. The first sick day resets the count to zero, so one miss reads as total failure, and that's when people quit. Every day with no rest also makes a miss almost certain. Rewrite it: three runs a week, on named days and times, with an if-then for illness, and an easy restart session. The classic mistake is thinking specific means safe.

So, to close the gap, set a process goal, decide when, where and how, record it, and judge setbacks by the plan, not the person. But self-regulation is something you do alone. Here's a plan: Tuesday, six am, the park. Someone else keeps that plan, and so do dozens of others. Why do people turn up to a bootcamp they don't enjoy?
